topic: Custom tool integrations using model context protocols

components.title: Architecture of Model Context Protocol (MCP) clients and servers
components.teaches: Students will understand the client-server architecture of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and how LLM agent workspaces communicate with external tools. They will identify the roles of host applications, MCP clients, and MCP servers during session initialization and tool exposure.

components.title: JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol format for tool discovery and calls
components.teaches: Students will learn how JSON-RPC 2.0 messages are structured for tools/list and tools/call requests in MCP. They will examine request IDs, method headers, parameter payloads, and response objects transmitted over standard streams.

components.title: Defining strict input JSON schemas for MCP tools
components.teaches: Students will learn how to write precise JSON Schema definitions for tool parameters to guide LLM tool calling. They will specify required fields, parameter data types, descriptions, and validation constraints that prevent ambiguous agent invocations.

components.title: Implementing an MCP server using an official SDK
components.teaches: Students will walk through building a lightweight MCP server using an official SDK. They will observe how decorated functions are exposed as callable tools and how incoming JSON arguments are parsed automatically.

components.title: Activity: Writing and running a custom MCP server tool
components.teaches: Students will write a custom tool function on an MCP server that executes local file or system operations and returns formatted content blocks. They will test the server execution using standard input streams to verify correct responses.

components.title: Configuring workspace settings to discover custom MCP servers
components.teaches: Students will configure an agent workspace JSON configuration file to register their custom server executable and command-line arguments. They will verify that the agent successfully discovers and surfaces the new tool capabilities.

components.title: Handling execution errors and returning structured MCP errors
components.teaches: Students will learn how to catch internal tool execution failures and map them to structured MCP error responses using the isError flag. They will distinguish between runtime exceptions inside tool execution and protocol-level transport failures.

Secure your MCP server using Descope for free: https://descope.plug.dev/W4lLipY

MCP servers are quickly becoming one of the most important pieces of the AI ecosystem. But what actually happens behind the scenes?

In this video, I break down MCP servers from the ground up and then build one from scratch. We’ll cover what MCP is, how local and remote servers differ, how access control works, and how the MCP protocol connects AI models to external tools and data.

Then we’ll put it all together by building an MCP server and adding authentication so you can see how these systems work in practice. If you’re building AI agents or want to understand how AI connects to real-world tools, this is a great place to start.

notebooklm_sources.title: How Model Context Protocol (MCP) actually works
notebooklm_sources.description:
Google MCPs → https://goo.gle/3PYkjky 
Build an ADK agent with Google MCPs → https://goo.gle/4o6h8DP 
Connect an MCP server to an AI agent → https://goo.gle/4uk7YW2 

APIs were built for deterministic programs, but AI models reason probabilistically. So how do you get your AI agents to talk to your tools and data without writing messy, custom integration code every time? Enter the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In this video, Smitha Kolan explains what MCP is, how it standardizes the way AI models discover and interact with external resources, and why it's becoming the new standard over traditional APIs for AI-powered applications

Chapters:
0:00 - Intro: The problem with APIs and AI 
0:48 - What is Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
1:26 - What exactly do MCPs connect to? 
2:43 - How MCP works (clients vs. servers) 
4:03 - MCP core components: Tools, prompts, resources & context 
5:20 - MCP vs. API: What is the difference? 
6:43 - Practical example: Building an AI assistant using MCP 
7:48 - Summary
